newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASEAN delays decision on Cambodian membership.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN delays decision on Cambodian membership.

text.p: ASEAN on Monday delayed a decision on when to let Cambodia join the organisation but said the country's admission, deferred by recent political turmoil, was just a formality.

"Cambodia is part of Southeast Asia. The timing for actual membership is just a formality," Philippines foreign minister Domingo Siazon told a news conference after a meeting of foreign ministers of the nine-member grouping.

Indonesian foreign minister Ali Alatas said Norodom Ranariddh, who was ousted as First Prime Minister last month, remained "a very important figure as the leader of one of the political parties" in Cambodia.
But ASEAN would not challenge action by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen to arrest Ranariddh if he returned home, Alatas told the news conference.
The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) postponed Cambodia's membership last month after Ranariddh was ousted by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen after two days of bloody fighting.
ASEAN's problem of what to do with Cambodia is complex. It has long aimed to group all 10 Southeast Asian countries to form the world's fourth-largest trading bloc.
But it does not want to appear to be siding with one of the factions in Cambodia's internal tussle.

The ASEAN dilemma was further complicated on Saturday by Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk, who said he regarded Ung Huot, elected First Prime Minister to replace Ranariddh, as a puppet and that his son, Ranariddh, was still premier.
But the king, who reigns but does not rule, also authorised acting head of state Chea Sim to appoint Ung Huot in Ranariddh's place.
Asked by reporters when Cambodia would join the grouping, Siazon said: "There's really no answer to that."
"Later or sooner are really relative terms. It didn't happen today. It won't happen tomorrow. It depends on further developments," he added.
ASEAN currently groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Cambodia was scheduled to join along with Burma and Laos last month, but its induction was postponed because of the turmoil that followed the violent overthrow of Ranariddh by Hun Sen on July 6 after clashes in the capital Phnom Penh.

Siazon said it was essential that political stability returned to Cambodia before it could be admitted into ASEAN. The holding of free and fair elections, previously scheduled for May 1998, were vital indicators of stability, he added.
"As of today we still have some fighting going on in some parts of Cambodia. Clearly there is still some political destabilisation," Siazon said.
"For the future of Cambodia, it is important to have free and fair elections in May, where all political forces can play a part."
In the meantime ASEAN would continue to "engage" Hun Sen and Ung Huot, now firmly in control of Cambodia, as the organisation recognised countries not governments, he said.

"ASEAN is taking a realistic view of the situation, in terms of the power configuration in Cambodia," Julius Parrenas, executive director of the think-tank Centre for Research and Communication in Manila, said before Monday's meeting.
"They will have to take the present reality as a starting point. His (Hun Sen's) military forces practically control Cambodia."
